title: Short Stuff: Ramree Island Crocodile Massacre
summary: Short Stuff episode (hosted with Ben sitting in for Dave) debunking the Ramree Island crocodile massacre legend, in which roughly 900 Japanese soldiers were supposedly eaten by saltwater crocodiles in a mangrove swamp off Burma (now Myanmar) in 1945. The hosts trace the story to Royal Canadian Lieutenant Bruce Wright, a frogman leader and wildlife biologist whose 1962 book Wildlife Sketches Near and Far recounted it only briefly and second-hand; later Roger Caras (spelled Karris in the transcript) repeated it in Dangerous to Man. They cover saltwater crocodile facts and attack statistics, historian Frank McLynn's objection that the story offends historical verifiability, official records that never mention it, post-war investigations with Burmese villagers suggesting perhaps a dozen were eaten, and the actual event: on February 18, 1945, Japanese soldiers drowned or were machine-gunned by British forces while swimming from Ramree Island to the mainland, and some were killed by sharks or died when boats sank.
topics: Guinness Book of World Records myth

segments.title: Opening and introduction of the crocodile massacre story
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode about the Ramree Island crocodile massacre and Chuck lays out the claim that about 900 of 1,000 Japanese soldiers were eaten by crocodiles in 1945.

segments.title: Origins of the story and Bruce Wright
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why the story was believed, and how Royal Canadian Lieutenant Bruce Wright, a frogman leader and wildlife biologist, wrote a brief account of it in his 1962 book Wildlife Sketches Near and Far.
topics: Guinness Book of World Records myth

segments.title: Credibility of sources and second-hand account
segments.summary: Roger Caras repeated the story in Dangerous to Man. The hosts note Wright was on the island but did not witness the event himself, having heard it second-hand from British soldiers.

segments.title: Saltwater crocodiles and attack statistics
segments.summary: The hosts describe the saltwater crocodile, its size and aggression, and cite 2015 figures of 79 fatal attacks out of 180 in Southeast Asia, coastal India and Oceania, arguing that 900 deaths in one night is implausible.

segments.title: Historians challenge the story and official records
segments.summary: Historian Frank McLynn said the story offends historical verifiability. Official Japanese and British records don't mention it, and post-war investigations with Burmese villagers suggest most soldiers died of disease, dehydration and exposure, with perhaps a dozen eaten.

segments.title: What actually happened: drowning, machine guns and sharks
segments.summary: Stephen Platt and a Nazi World War Weird investigation found British military records of February 18, 1945, when Japanese soldiers swimming from Ramree Island to the mainland were drowned, machine-gunned by the British, or killed by sharks, and some died when boats sank. Crocodiles fed on bodies the next day, helping the legend grow.

segments.title: Summary of how the legend formed
segments.summary: Josh sums up how the facts were combined with Bruce Wright's account to form the crocodile massacre legend and calls the myth busted.

segments.title: Sign-off and credits
segments.summary: Closing lines and a production credit.
